author: A Robot
objectives: Students will determine the steric number of a central atom from its Lewis structure by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Students will predict the electron-domain geometry of a molecule from its steric number, identifying the linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral arrangement.
Students will distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry, and identify the molecular shape produced when one or more domains is a lone pair.
Students will explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, and predict the direction of bond-angle deviations from idealized values.
Students will apply VSEPR predictions to specific molecules and compare predicted geometries to experimentally observed structures.

modules.description: Introduction to VSEPR theory and the concept of electron-pair repulsion as the driving force behind molecular geometry
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Understand the core principle of VSEPR theory: electron pairs repel each other and arrange to minimize repulsion
Learn to count electron domains (bonding pairs and lone pairs) from a Lewis structure
Recognize that electron-domain geometry depends on the steric number
instructions: Watch as the central atom and electron domains are introduced
Observe how the electron domains arrange themselves in space
Notice the relationship between the number of electron domains and their spatial arrangement

clips.changeMeaning: Establish the laboratory setting by displaying the central atom and introducing the concept of electron domains. The atoms and domains are shown in a simple initial configuration to set context for the theory.
clips.narration: VSEPR theory is based on a simple but powerful idea: electron pairs around a central atom repel each other. These pairs will arrange themselves in three-dimensional space to get as far apart as possible, minimizing repulsion. This arrangement determines the shape of the molecule.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the relationship between Lewis structure information and electron domain counting. A connecting line between central atom and domains visualizes bonding, preparing students for the steric number concept.
clips.narration: We count electron domains by identifying all electron pairs around the central atom. This includes bonding pairs — electrons shared with other atoms — and lone pairs — electrons not involved in bonding. The total number of electron domains is called the steric number.

clips.changeMeaning: Demonstrate how electron domains repel and reorganize spatially. The two-domain linear case is shown, establishing the geometric principle before moving to more complex cases.
clips.narration: To minimize repulsion, electron pairs space themselves as far apart as possible. With two electron domains, they point in opposite directions — a linear arrangement. With three domains, they adopt a trigonal planar geometry, 120 degrees apart. With four, they form a tetrahedral shape at approximately 109.5 degrees. These fundamental shapes are the electron-domain geometries.

modules.moduleName: Electron-Domain Geometries: The Five Fundamental Shapes
modules.description: Exploration of the five fundamental electron-domain geometries and how they arise from the repulsion of electron pairs
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify and visualize each of the five fundamental electron-domain geometries
Predict electron-domain geometry based on steric number
Understand how steric number 2 through 6 produces linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral geometries respectively
instructions: Observe each electron-domain geometry as it is presented
Note the characteristic angles and spatial arrangement in each case
Think about how the geometry changes as more electron domains are added

clips.changeMeaning: Present the linear geometry with two domains positioned opposite each other. This establishes the simplest case and provides a foundation for understanding more complex geometries.
clips.narration: Let's start with steric number two: two electron domains around a central atom. To maximize distance between them, they point in opposite directions, 180 degrees apart. This is a linear electron-domain geometry.

clips.changeMeaning: Transition to trigonal planar geometry. A third domain is activated and positioned above the central atom, with all three now arranged in a planar triangle.
clips.narration: With three electron domains, steric number three, the domains arrange themselves in a flat triangle. Each domain is 120 degrees away from its neighbors. This is trigonal planar geometry. All three domains lie in the same plane.

clips.changeMeaning: Demonstrate tetrahedral geometry by positioning four domains toward the corners of a tetrahedron. This is a key geometry that appears frequently in organic molecules.
clips.narration: Four electron domains, steric number four, adopt a tetrahedral shape. Imagine a tetrahedron — a four-sided pyramid. The four domains point toward the corners of this tetrahedron, with bond angles of approximately 109.5 degrees. This is the tetrahedral electron-domain geometry, one of the most common in organic chemistry.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the two highest-steric-number geometries: trigonal bipyramidal (5 domains) and octahedral (6 domains). These prepare students for more complex molecules in the next module.
clips.narration: With five electron domains, steric number five, we get trigonal bipyramidal geometry — imagine two triangular pyramids glued base-to-base. With six electron domains, steric number six, we get octahedral geometry — six domains pointing toward the corners of an octahedron, with 90-degree angles between adjacent pairs. These two geometries are less common but important for transition metals and certain main-group elements.

modules.moduleName: From Electron Geometry to Molecular Geometry: The Role of Lone Pairs
modules.description: Understanding how lone pairs modify the electron-domain geometry to produce the actual molecular geometry, and why lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry
Predict molecular geometry when lone pairs are present in the electron-domain arrangement
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, leading to bond-angle compression
Predict bond-angle deviations from idealized values based on lone pair interactions
instructions: Observe how lone pairs affect the spatial arrangement of bonding pairs
Notice how the molecular geometry differs from the electron-domain geometry when lone pairs are present
Pay attention to the relative sizes of lone pairs versus bonding pairs

components.text: Electron geometry: Tetrahedral | Molecular geometry: Bent

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce water as the primary example, showing the central oxygen atom with two bonding pairs (to hydrogen atoms) and two lone pairs. This sets up the comparison between electron geometry and molecular geometry.
clips.narration: Here's a crucial distinction in VSEPR theory: the electron-domain geometry describes the arrangement of all electron pairs — both bonding and lone pairs. The molecular geometry describes only the arrangement of atoms — we ignore the lone pairs' positions. Water is a perfect example. Oxygen has four electron domains: two bonding pairs and two lone pairs. The electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral, based on the steric number of four.

clips.changeMeaning: Visually emphasize the size difference between lone pairs and bonding pairs. The lone pairs are drawn larger to represent their greater repulsive effect, preparing students for the concept of bond-angle compression.
clips.narration: But lone pairs are different from bonding pairs. A lone pair occupies space around the central atom just like a bonding pair does, but it is not shared with another atom. Because it is concentrated on one atom, the lone pair repels other electron pairs more strongly than a bonding pair does. The electron clouds of lone pairs are less polarized and take up more angular space.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the actual bent molecular geometry of water by repositioning the bonding pairs closer together to illustrate the 104.5° bond angle, compared to the idealized 109.5° of tetrahedral geometry.
clips.narration: Because the two lone pairs on oxygen repel strongly, they push the two bonding pairs closer together. In the tetrahedral electron-domain geometry, we would expect a 109.5-degree bond angle, but in water, the actual H-O-H bond angle is 104.5 degrees — compressed by about 5 degrees due to lone pair repulsion. The molecular geometry of water is bent, not tetrahedral, because we only count the positions of the atoms, not the lone pairs.

modules.moduleName: Molecular Shapes and Applications: From NH₃ to SF₆
modules.description: Application of VSEPR theory to specific molecules, comparing predicted geometries to experimentally observed structures and understanding the importance of geometry in molecular properties
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply VSEPR theory systematically: draw Lewis structure, count electron domains, predict electron-domain geometry, identify molecular geometry
Explain how molecular geometry influences properties like polarity, reactivity, and intermolecular interactions
Recognize the full set of common molecular shapes arising from different steric numbers and numbers of lone pairs
instructions: As each molecule is introduced, try to predict its geometry before the answer is revealed
Compare the electron-domain geometry to the molecular geometry in each case
Note how the presence and number of lone pairs changes the molecular shape

clips.changeMeaning: Present ammonia as the first real-molecule example. Show that NH₃ has a trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry despite tetrahedral electron-domain geometry, demonstrating the importance of lone pair effects.
clips.narration: Let's apply VSEPR theory to ammonia, NH₃. Nitrogen has five valence electrons. It forms three bonding pairs with hydrogen atoms and has one lone pair. That's four electron domains total — steric number four. So the electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral. But with one lone pair, the molecular geometry becomes trigonal pyramidal. The lone pair sits at one corner of the tetrahedron, and the three hydrogen atoms form a triangular pyramid around it.

clips.changeMeaning: Show methane and water alongside ammonia to highlight how the number of lone pairs (0, 1, or 2) changes the molecular geometry from tetrahedral to trigonal pyramidal to bent, even though all three have tetrahedral electron-domain geometry.
clips.narration: Compare this to methane, CH₄. Carbon has four valence electrons and forms four bonding pairs with hydrogen. No lone pairs — steric number four. Both the electron-domain geometry and the molecular geometry are tetrahedral, with perfect 109.5-degree bond angles. Water, H₂O, sits in between: two bonding pairs, two lone pairs, steric number four, but the molecular geometry is bent. The differences in geometry reflect differences in electron pair composition.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce SF₆ as an example of octahedral geometry, showing how VSEPR theory extends to higher steric numbers and more complex molecules. This emphasizes the power and universality of the VSEPR framework.
clips.narration: For molecules with higher steric numbers, VSEPR predicts shapes like seesaw, T-shaped, square planar, and square pyramidal. Sulfur hexafluoride, SF₆, is an extreme example: sulfur is the central atom with six bonding pairs and no lone pairs, giving steric number six and octahedral geometry. These predictions agree remarkably well with experimental structures determined by X-ray crystallography and electron diffraction.
